title: Technology delivery: Routine relief creates strategic capacity
desc: Offers operational examples of integrated service delivery while separating promotional claims from independent evidence of reliability.

kps.k: The central proposition is that technology-enabled delivery can relieve routine legal workload and create capacity for strategic work, rather than simply replace lawyers.
kps.d: The material presents three distinct routes: business self-service that reduces requests reaching legal, software that assists lawyers, and outsourced services combining professionals, technology and project management. Klinger links Moderna’s contract self-service to more sophisticated legal work; McDonnell distinguishes time savings that indirectly enable strategy from direct strategic applications such as tariff scenario planning. These accounts describe capacity creation, not proof that every saved hour becomes strategic value or that legal roles disappear.

qs.q: So we’re seeing that customers are using it as a way to facilitate getting to that higher order critical thinking strategic planning and so it may seem a little more indirect.
qs.a: Laura Clayton McDonnell on Legal Technology, AI, and Corporate Transformation at Thomson Reuters · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: I mean, I think at least now we're in this phenomenal, hopefully long intermediate phase where the software is picking up a lot of the heavy lifting on the things we don't want to do as lawyers, giving us more time to do the things we do.
qs.a: The Rise of the Legal Technologist · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Workflow integration and organisational preparation feature as practical mechanisms for adoption.
kps.d: Dunlop describes Summize contract creation and review submission inside Teams, Slack, email and CRM applications; Stevenson describes Spellbook’s drafting and review assistance inside Word. These serve different users: business staff seeking self-service and lawyers using a copilot. The Salesforce interviewer recommends considering existing business tools, but the excerpt contains no answer about Salesforce’s own legal team. Kildow stresses shared client objectives across teams, while Twigger recommends planning around recurring cases, data and clients’ internal expertise. Together, these claims locate implementation work in processes and coordination, not model capability alone.

qs.q: They can create contracts or submit contracts for review, but using the tools that they already use.
qs.a: From Athlete to AI: Summize CEO's Legal Tech Entrepreneurial Journey (Tom Dunlop) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: So Spellbook was our generative AI co-pilot for transactional lawyers and built right into Microsoft Word.
qs.a: How a Start-Up's Legal Bills Led to Spellbook, an AI Co-Pilot for Transactional Lawyers (Scott Stevenson - Co-Founder) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: Reported operational gains provide concrete examples, but their measures and evidential limits differ.
kps.d: Klinger says Moderna’s contract-specific GPTs answer 90% of business users’ questions, without explaining measurement. McDonnell reports more than an 80% reduction in Thomson Reuters’ internal contract review time and millions in outside-counsel savings at an unnamed Legal Tracker customer. Separately, the Ironclad speaker reports 80% faster contract turnaround without a baseline, sample or method. These figures concern different outcomes and cannot be pooled or attributed uniformly to generative AI. In the Anna Guo interview, the interviewer restates a study claim that AI matched or exceeded lawyers on reliable contract first drafts; the excerpt supplies no numerical results or methodology and does not establish autonomous completion of legal work.

qs.q: So they’ve leveraged our products and they’ve been able to reduce contract review time by 80 % plus.
qs.a: Laura Clayton McDonnell on Legal Technology, AI, and Corporate Transformation at Thomson Reuters · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: And the benefits that we have proven at this point is, one, speed, those lawyers can turn around contracts 80% faster, which is a tremendous result for the business because one of the things that we talk about at Ironclad a lot, and I think our customers really appreciate, is behind every business process is a contract process.
qs.a: The Rise of the Legal Technologist · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Percipient’s recurring promotion advances a service-delivery proposition, not independent corroboration of interviewees’ AI claims.
kps.d: The advertisement markets legal operations, contracts, subpoena compliance and document review through legal professionals using technology, project management and human oversight. Its survey references are unspecified, and its 100,000-document subpoena illustrates a hypothetical burden rather than a completed engagement. Repetition across interviews adds no evidence of savings or guest endorsement, and the pitch does not consistently establish that the technology is AI. A separate promotion announces a subpoena service planned for 2026, promising validity checks, issue flagging, collaborative data preparation and portal tracking. Its advance cost-collection promise applies only where charging the requesting party is permitted.

qs.q: By combining legal expertise and technology, Percipient enables legal teams to get more work done for less.
qs.a: Future-Proofing Legal Ops: AI Literacy, Innovation and Augmentation (Meredith Kildow, President Consilio) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: I just wanted to give you a heads up about a new service Percipient is rolling out in 2026, subpoena compliance services.
qs.a: Bridging Law Firm Silos: How Law Firms Can Maximize AI-Driven Cross-Selling (James Barclay, CEO Passle) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: The main tension concerns demonstrated use and reliability versus product ambitions, rather than a developed dispute over whether technology has value.
kps.d: The Kildow interviewer challenges future-facing AI hype and requests present uses; the Fitzpatrick interviewer asks how LexisNexis will preserve reliability. Neither supplied excerpt includes the answer. Fitzpatrick describes current drafting and document-analysis functions but presents portfolio-wide, personalised assistance as a vision. Klinger separately predicts supervised contract and e-discovery agents performing tasks previously assigned to people by the end of the year of her remarks; neither deployment nor security is demonstrated in that forecast. These distinctions make current functionality, verified output quality, realised savings and future autonomy separate questions for buyers.

qs.q: But what are you really seeing, you internally, what you guys are doing, but clients, how is it really actually being used today?
qs.a: Future-Proofing Legal Ops: AI Literacy, Innovation and Augmentation (Meredith Kildow, President Consilio) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: That being said, how do you approach innovation AI specifically in this what we're talking about today to add to the products you already have but while maintaining the reliabilities people used the Lexus Nexus, you know, they've been used, I'm sure many people have used it for years and years and years.
qs.a: Sean Fitzpatrick — LexisNexis (CEO, North America/UK/Ireland) on Protégé, the OpenAI Agreement and Augmentation Not Replacement · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

kps.k: The proposed payoff extends beyond throughput, but strategic contribution and human relationships remain distinct from automation itself.
kps.d: Ziniti’s personal account presents legal as helping a business move faster and shape strategy, without establishing an AI effect. Tsakalakis recommends reinvesting time released by automation in client and referral relationships, qualifying his advice by role, firm size and practice area; his prediction that automation costs will approach zero remains speculative. Passle’s biography-based content matching offers a complementary tool for discovering colleagues and expertise, not measured cross-selling gains. The practical implication is to specify what freed capacity should accomplish and assess that outcome separately from tool adoption or task speed.

qs.q: Being a part of that and seeing how legal could contribute to the business moving faster, reaching more people, really strategy, that was what that job taught me.
qs.a: Cecilia Ziniti — GC AI (Founder & CEO, former General Counsel) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: This is going to vary depending on your role in the firm, and size of firm, and practice area, and all this stuff.
qs.a: Do What the Bots Cannot: How AI Is Reshaping Legal Marketing, Data Analysis and Biz Dev, But Not the Human Connection (Gyi Tsakalakis, AttorneySync) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

vlens.an: These selected in-house counsel and legal-operations sources accept the proposition that technology-enabled delivery can remove routine workload and increase capacity for higher-value work. They build on it by identifying practical delivery mechanisms: contract self-service for business users, integration with tools already used by the business, and service models combining legal professionals, technology, project management and human oversight. The strongest operational account is Klinger’s report that Moderna’s contract-specific GPTs answer many routine questions, accelerate turnaround and free the legal team for more strategic and sophisticated work. Material variation concerns evidential strength and maturity: Klinger distinguishes a current self-service use case from forecast contract and e-discovery agents, whose deployment and security benefits were not yet demonstrated; the other source relies partly on Percipient’s promotional, unquantified efficiency claims and an interviewer’s suggestion about existing business tools, without showing that saved capacity actually becomes strategic value. Thus, the voice constructively develops the proposition while preserving a distinction between demonstrated workflows, marketing claims and anticipated agentic capabilities. Because the corpus is curated, these accounts should not be treated as representative of all in-house counsel or legal-operations professionals.

qs.q: But also, I think so often legal departments overlook using the tools they already have at their disposal and at the business started using.
qs.a: From 'No' to 'Go': How AI Guardrails Drive Trust, Enabling Legal to be a Business Accelerant, Not Blocker (Sabastian Niles, Salesforce President & CLO) · In-house counsel · 2025

vlens.an: This curated legal-tech vendor voice accepts the proposition that technology should augment legal work by reducing routine workload and enabling higher-value activity, and materially develops it through concrete delivery mechanisms. These include business self-service embedded in existing applications, lawyer-facing copilots, personalised knowledge discovery, and outsourced services combining legal professionals, technology, project management and human oversight. Several sources further specify that successful adoption requires workflow-specific planning, use of existing client expertise and organisational alignment; others identify intended uses of released capacity, including strategic planning, legal thinking and relationship development. Material internal variation concerns the strength and scope of the evidence. McDonnell directly links contract-review savings to strategic work and scenario planning, while Summize, Spellbook and Protégé mainly describe capabilities without demonstrating that saved time became strategic value. Ironclad and Thomson Reuters report substantial operational gains, but methodological detail or independent validation is limited. Percipient’s repeated claims are promotional and do not become stronger through repetition, and some product ambitions remain future-facing or leave reliability questions unanswered. The sources therefore strengthen the proposition chiefly with implementation detail and illustrative examples, not general proof that automation reliably produces strategic capacity in every setting.

qs.q: And that mail includes drafting agreements and doing contract review and  providing advice and what we’re seeing, especially if we use sort of Thomson Reuters General Counsel’s office as an example, if they can reduce the time it takes to review a contract, that could free up time for them to do more strategic work.
qs.a: Laura Clayton McDonnell on Legal Technology, AI, and Corporate Transformation at Thomson Reuters · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: But if you just get a plan for the cases that you handle, the types of data that you see on a regular basis and work directly with your clients and whatever expertise they already have to do that internally, you can do it a lot more effectively.
qs.a: Minerva 26 CEO Kelly Twigger on Leading E-Discovery into the AI Age · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

vlens.an: This curated source supports the proposition only through the separate Percipient promotional segment, which presents technology-enabled, human-supervised legal delivery as a way to increase legal-team capacity and reduce cost across routine operational work. That aligns with relieving workload rather than replacing lawyers, although it does not demonstrate that the resulting capacity is actually redirected to strategic work. The evidential basis is limited: the claims are promotional, the referenced surveys and performance measures are unspecified, and no independent reliability or savings data are supplied. There is also material internal divergence within the source: Rosario’s substantive interview focuses on decentralized AI’s funding, permissionless access and geopolitical risks, so it neither materially supports nor contests the legal-delivery proposition. Despite the facet label, the source does not connect these efficiency claims to access to justice or unmet civil legal need; its legal discussion concerns provider-side services for legal teams.

qs.q: By combining legal expertise and technology, Percipient enables legal teams to get more work done for less.
qs.a: Nelson Rosario on Decentralized AI: An Alternative to Big Tech or a Complimentary Approach? · Access to justice · 2025

qs.q: Our team of legal professionals leverage tech and project management principles with the right amount of human oversight to deliver precise, efficient, and cost-effective legal solutions.
qs.a: Nelson Rosario on Decentralized AI: An Alternative to Big Tech or a Complimentary Approach? · Access to justice · 2025

vlens.an: This curated market-analyst, consultancy and press source supports the proposition, but only through a promotional segment rather than independent evidence. Percipient is presented as taking over document-production legwork and integrating data preparation, status, deadlines and metrics in a secure portal, thereby allowing the legal team to concentrate on core work. This is directly consistent with routine relief creating strategic capacity and provides a concrete workflow example. Materially, however, the source does not demonstrate realised capacity gains, reliability or even that the relevant technology is AI. Most of the underlying discussion instead concerns predicted regulatory difficulty around AI legal advice and chatbot disclaimers, which neither supports nor contradicts the delivery proposition. The source therefore supports the proposition modestly rather than extending it.

qs.q: Basically, Percipient handles legwork so your team can focus on the core work.
qs.a: The Uberization of UPL? How AI Is Outpacing the Unauthorized Practice of Law (Ken Crutchfield, Bill Henderson, Jim Doppke) · Market & press · 2026

qs.q: You'll see everything in Percipient's secure portal, status, due dates, metrics, all of it.
qs.a: The Uberization of UPL? How AI Is Outpacing the Unauthorized Practice of Law (Ken Crutchfield, Bill Henderson, Jim Doppke) · Market & press · 2026

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources collectively accept the proposition that technology-enabled delivery should relieve routine legal work and augment lawyers, and they materially develop it with concrete adoption mechanisms. These include contract self-service for business users, copilots embedded in lawyers’ existing tools, workflow integration with email, collaboration and CRM platforms, and supervised services combining legal professionals, technology and project management. The strongest operational accounts connect routine relief to strategic capacity: Klinger reports that Moderna’s contract-specific GPTs answer many business questions while freeing lawyers for more sophisticated work, and McDonnell links reduced contract-review time to higher-order planning while identifying tariff scenario planning as a direct strategic use. Other sources specify organisational prerequisites, including planning around recurring matters and data, using clients’ internal expertise, and aligning delivery teams around shared outcomes. Material variation concerns evidential strength and maturity rather than disagreement over the proposition. Reported customer or internal examples offer concrete but incompletely documented gains; product vendors mainly describe capabilities and ambitions; and Percipient’s repeated efficiency claims are promotional material rather than independent corroboration. Current augmentation and self-service are also distinct from Klinger’s forecast of supervised agents performing work previously assigned to people. Reliability and demonstrated present use remain unresolved in excerpts that raise those questions without supplying answers. Tsakalakis further extends the proposition by arguing that released capacity should be deliberately reinvested in relationships, while Ziniti describes strategic legal contribution without establishing that technology caused it. The decentralized-AI discussion is largely peripheral. No supplied source clearly rejects technology-enabled routine relief, but the corpus does not establish that every efficiency gain becomes strategic value or that the reported outcomes generalise beyond the cited examples.

qs.q: And that mail includes drafting agreements and doing contract review and  providing advice and what we’re seeing, especially if we use sort of Thomson Reuters General Counsel’s office as an example, if they can reduce the time it takes to review a contract, that could free up time for them to do more strategic work.
qs.a: Laura Clayton McDonnell on Legal Technology, AI, and Corporate Transformation at Thomson Reuters · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources support the proposition that technology-enabled delivery can absorb routine or operational work and preserve human capacity for higher-value activity. The clearest support comes from The Rise of the Legal Technologist, which frames software as performing document-heavy work so lawyers can spend more time on legal thinking and reports faster in-house contracting. Percipient’s recurring promotion similarly presents a managed subpoena workflow—data preparation, portal tracking and related legwork—as freeing legal teams for core work. Passle extends the capacity logic into knowledge and colleague discovery, while Descrybe characterises AI as amplifying experienced expertise rather than straightforwardly replacing skilled people. Material variation lies primarily in evidential strength and relevance: the Ironclad performance figure is vendor-reported without disclosed methodology; Passle offers no measured cross-selling outcome; Percipient’s 2026 service is promotional and future-facing, with repetition across sources providing no independent corroboration; and Descrybe’s developer-productivity observation is qualitative rather than evidence about legal workload. The UPL discussion is largely orthogonal, offering predictions about regulatory difficulty rather than testing the delivery proposition. Overall, these sources accept the capacity-creation framing, but mostly illustrate claimed mechanisms and intended benefits rather than independently verified reliability or realised strategic value.

qs.q: I mean, I think at least now we're in this phenomenal, hopefully long intermediate phase where the software is picking up a lot of the heavy lifting on the things we don't want to do as lawyers, giving us more time to do the things we do.
